sources.citation: Afrika und Übersee, OJS site (Hamburg University Press), backlist and archive pages,https://journals.sub.uni-hamburg.de/hup1/afrikaunduebersee/backlist
sources.note: Establishes access status: 'Volumes 1–92 are not yet available in digital form'; open-access archive begins with Vol. 93 (2020). Sibomana 1986/1988/1989 (vols 69, 71, 72) are therefore print-only.
Lists Sibomana 1986 as the only source; no feature values were rendered on the page (no stress/tone/syllable features visible).

sources.citation: Glottolog 5.x languoid page nkem1242 and reference records 319477 (Blench 2014 Ekoid ms.) and 701778 (Ethnologue 28),https://glottolog.org/resource/languoid/id/nkem1242
sources.note: Only Sibomana 1986 (grammar sketch), Blench 2014 (overview/comparative/wordlist) and Ethnologue listed; nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Blench, Roger M. (2011 circulation draft; Glottolog cites as 2014 ms., 27 pp.). Ekoid: Bantoid languages of the Nigeria-Cameroun borderland. Cambridge: Kay Williamson Educational Foundation.
sources.note: Section 3 Phonology (printed p. 5-6, p. 7-8) is family-level and comparative: proto-Ekoid consonants, seven vowels, and 'Both Mbe and Ekoid have High, Low, Rising, Falling and Downstep tones' (printed p. 6). No mention of stress or accent for Nkem or any Ekoid lect; Nkim and Nkum appear only as columns in the comparative wordlist (Appendix I). archived copy (Internet Archive, 5 Apr 2022) because rogerblench.info is could not be reached by automated download.

sources.citation: Yoder, Zachariah, Katarína Hannelová & Linus Otronyi (2008). A Summary of the Sociolinguistic Survey of the Bakor languages of Cross River State, Nigeria (24 Sept 2008), with Appendix 2 Bakor wordlists (30 pp.). Composite PDF hosted by R. Blench.
sources.note: Sociolinguistic survey (intelligibility, vitality) plus tone-marked 345-word lists for Nkim (Adagom) and Nkum (Alladim) among nine Bakor lects. No phonology section; a full-text search for stress/accent yields nothing but 'stone'. archived copy (Internet Archive, 26 May 2025).

sources.citation: Sibomana, Leo (1986). An outline of Nkem language. Afrika und Übersee 69: 251-292.

sources.access_detail: a digital copy exists, behind a library sign-; also held in print at Harvard (Widener Library, call number Philol 14)
sources.note: The only grammar sketch of Nkem-Nkum (Glottolog's sole descriptive reference and WALS's source); its phonology section should state the tone system and whether stress plays any role.

sources.citation: Sibomana, Leo (1989). The tonal system of Nkem. Afrika und Übersee 72: 255-272.
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.access_detail: print only (no digital copy found when the work was looked up)
sources.note: Dedicated 18-page description of Nkem word prosody by the only linguist to have published a description of the language; the most likely place for an explicit statement on tone vs. stress at word level.

sources.citation: Sibomana, Leo (1988). Nkem folktales. Afrika und Übersee 71: 17-55.

sources.note: Tone-marked Nkem texts by the same author; would show whether any stress/accent marking is used in running text, and its introduction may summarize the prosodic system.

sources.citation: Asinya, O.E. (1987). A reconstruction of the segmental phonology of Bakor (an Ekoid Bantu language). MA thesis, University of Port Harcourt.

sources.note: Nigeria-based phonological study of the Bakor cluster (which includes Nkim/Nkum); segmental in focus but a phonology thesis may open with a suprasegmental statement.

sources.citation: Crabb, David W. (1965). Ekoid Bantu languages of Ogoja, Eastern Nigeria. Part 1: Introduction, phonology and comparative vocabulary. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.

sources.note: Only book-length phonological treatment covering Nkim and Nkum (as Ekoid lects) with tone-marked comparative vocabulary; may contain a general prosodic statement for the Ekoid group.
